19.6.3.5 Using Oxygen Nucleophiles

Water and alcohols are oxygen nucleophiles. They can add to carbonyl group to form addition products.

a. Using Water

When aldehydes or ketones react with water, they add a water molecule and form geminal diols (1,1-diols). The reaction is called hydration and can be catalyzed by acid or any hydroxide base.

b. Using Alcohol

Like water, alcohol also adds reversibly to carbonyl group, in the presence of acid catalyst and initially forms an addition product, generally called hemiacetal. Hemiacetal contains both hydroxyl and alkoxy groups bonded to same carbon. In the presence of excess of alcohol, hemiacetal reacts further to form acetal with removal of water. Acetal has two alkoxy group at the same carbon and are geminal diethers. Although hydration is catalyzed by either acid or base, acetal formation must be acid-catalyzed.

Aldehydes give more addition product at equilibrium than ketones.

19.6.4 Oxidation Reactions of Carbonyl Compounds

Both aldehydes and ketones undergo oxidation in the presence of oxidizing agents, however, aldehydes are more easily oxidized than ketones as the hydrogen atom attached to the carbonyl group in aldehydes is oxidized to –OH group.

Tidbit

Acetals formed from ketones are often called ketals, although this term has been dropped from the IUPAC nomenclature and the term acetal is now applied to the adducts of both aldehydes and ketones.

a. Oxidation of Aldehydes

Aldehydes are easily oxidized to carboxylic acids, in the presence of strong oxidizing agents like acidified permanganate or acidified dichromate, but also by mild oxidizing agents like Fehling’s solution, Benedict’s solution and Tollen’s reagent. Oxidation with strong oxidizing agents is already discussed in (Section 18.1.7.5). Oxidation with mild oxidizing agents such as Fehling’s solution, Benedict’s solution and Tollen’s reagent are used to distinguish aldehydes from ketones, as ketones are not oxidized by these reagents.

i. Tollen’s reagent test

Tollen’s reagent is ammonical silver nitrate and prepared by adding dilute solution of ammonia to solution of silver nitrate until the initially formed precipitate of silver(I) oxide dissolves. Ammonia forms a complex of diamminesilver(I) hydroxide ([Ag(NH₃)₂]OH) which is water soluble. When aldehyde is heated with this Tollen’s reagent, it oxidizes the aldehyde to corresponding carboxylate ion and the silver ion present in Tollen’s reagent, is reduced to metallic silver which deposits on the walls of test tube and forms a silver mirror. It is also called silver mirror test. Formation of silver mirror indicate the presence of aldehyde because ketone cannot be oxidized by Tollen’s reagent.

19.6.3.5 Using Oxygen Nucleophiles

Water and alcohols are oxygen nucleophiles. They can add to carbonyl group to form addition products.

a. Using Water

When aldehydes or ketones react with water, they add a water molecule and form geminal diols (1,1-diols). The reaction is called hydration and can be catalyzed by acid or any hydroxide base.

b. Using Alcohol

Like water, alcohol also adds reversibly to carbonyl group, in the presence of acid catalyst and initially forms an addition product, generally called hemiacetal. Hemiacetal contains both hydroxyl and alkoxy groups bonded to same carbon. In the presence of excess of alcohol, hemiacetal reacts further to form acetal with removal of water. Acetal has two alkoxy group at the same carbon and are geminal diethers. Although hydration is catalyzed by either acid or base, acetal formation must be acid-catalyzed.

Aldehydes give more addition product at equilibrium than ketones.

19.6.4 Oxidation Reactions of Carbonyl Compounds

Both aldehydes and ketones undergo oxidation in the presence of oxidizing agents, however, aldehydes are more easily oxidized than ketones as the hydrogen atom attached to the carbonyl group in aldehydes is oxidized to –OH group.

Tidbit

Acetals formed from ketones are often called ketals, although this term has been dropped from the IUPAC nomenclature and the term acetal is now applied to the adducts of both aldehydes and ketones.

a. Oxidation of Aldehydes

Aldehydes are easily oxidized to carboxylic acids, in the presence of strong oxidizing agents like acidified permanganate or acidified dichromate, but also by mild oxidizing agents like Fehling’s solution, Benedict’s solution and Tollen’s reagent. Oxidation with strong oxidizing agents is already discussed in (Section 18.1.7.5). Oxidation with mild oxidizing agents such as Fehling’s solution, Benedict’s solution and Tollen’s reagent are used to distinguish aldehydes from ketones, as ketones are not oxidized by these reagents.

i. Tollen’s reagent test

Tollen’s reagent is ammonical silver nitrate and prepared by adding dilute solution of ammonia to solution of silver nitrate until the initially formed precipitate of silver(I) oxide dissolves. Ammonia forms a complex of diamminesilver(I) hydroxide ([Ag(NH₃)₂]OH) which is water soluble. When aldehyde is heated with this Tollen’s reagent, it oxidizes the aldehyde to corresponding carboxylate ion and the silver ion present in Tollen’s reagent, is reduced to metallic silver which deposits on the walls of test tube and forms a silver mirror. It is also called silver mirror test. Formation of silver mirror indicate the presence of aldehyde because ketone cannot be oxidized by Tollen’s reagent.
